  • “I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers.
  • In a recent development, so, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A couple of years ago, Mr. Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.

I thought to myself at the time,.

“I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers. Onward to the next forty eight years of the Good Life!”.

In a recent development, so, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance. I had a marvelous time traveling everywhere and spending money like I thought a proper wealthy person would do.

I dined out in stylish restaurants, booked hotels based on their niceness rather than their cheapness, paid extra to sit in the “reduced torture” seats of the airplanes, and gave zero fucks about paying double for groceries if I happened to be in a Whole Foods rather than my usual Sam’s Club and Costco (and yes I treat myself to memberships at both warehouse stores!).

Among the highlights, my son and I have worked our way though a nice selection of late night EDM concerts and three Meowwolf art venues including a Christmas Day road trip from our winter home in Tempe Arizona to Las Vegas last year. And having spent much of the year as a single man, I had a wide open schedule to just meet up with friends, explore latest places and meet new people as opportunities came up. It felt like a year of adventurous transition, which means it felt like much more than twelve months.

Recent findings suggest that with all this flashy spending, I was sure my budget must have crept back into full American Consumer territory. But I was having too much fun to bother adding it all up to check.

Until recently, when I was doing another round of informal coaching for a friend and we both decided to tally our spending for the past year to compare notes.

When I finally finished sorting all of those transactions into a spreadsheet and hit the “sum” button, the results surprised me.

While my overall spending had indeed increased (especially in travel-related categories), the big-picture effect was still pretty minimal. Depending on how I account for things like the car and my business expenses, my spending went from $20,000 to about $30,000 (plus the usual hidden subsidy of a paid-off house.).

This level could still be sustained by a $1 million investment nest egg. Since my investments are quite a bit higher than that (especially after these recent years of crazy economic growth and the never-ending stock market rally), I’m still way under budget.

Although I still “failed” to really increase my spending to the MMM-recommended levels for old wealthy people, this still makes me happy, because I have genuinely had more fun with the abundance mindset, and I can keep trying more life experiments in the coming years.

As we covered in the 2019 article on the idea of an Optimization Council, it’s always a good idea to compare our spending, tips and tricks on how to get the most out of life. Almost twenty years into early retirement, this is where I have landed so far, although I’m always learning and open to feedback.

Anyway, let’s cut the wistful commentary and get into the budget.

Recent findings suggest that in summary: Wow, how interesting! When we compare this to my 2019 post on that year’s spending, it’s only a bit higher even after all the inflation we have seen in recent years. I spent more on travel and fun, but less on home renovation – partly because I was away so much I didn’t have as much time to work on my house. The health insurance is a newly introduced cost too since I was self-insured back then.

According to recent reports, my budget is notably missing the biggest expense for most people, which is housing costs. This is because I paid off my house long ago, and I also love working on and taking care of my own home, which means there are no bills for lawn mowing, plumbers, tree pruning or handyman services.

Industry observers note that this strategy is not for everyone, and it’s not even the optimum financial one for me – I would have been better off taking out the biggest mortgage I could get at 3% back in the sweet borrowing times of 2021, and putting all that principal to work in stock index funds where it would have almost doubled since then. But I still get a great peace of mind from just having no mortgage payment, and there’s really no better way to use your money than to buy such good feelings. Also, I get a secondary benefit of not having to buy house insurance, which saves me another $2000 per year, boosting my effective return on that payoff.

First of all, the biggest money saving factor of good health and good luck has continued, meaning I’ve still had no actual medical expenses. But I still do maintain two layers of health care support which together feel very much like the ultimate version of health insurance: a membership with a top of the line Direct Primary Care (DPC) medical clinic ($107 per month) plus a high-deductible blueprint ($201) with a health sharing organization called Sedera.

The combined cost of $308 per month is less than the cheapest Bronze proposal in the field of standard health insurance, yet I get personalized support with zero deductible for almost all typical medical needs, plus some protection from larger medical bills if my good luck runs out.

According to recent reports, but as a disclaimer, I’m not an expert on medical needs and health insurance because I’ve had so little experience with the system. And the highest priority in my life is arranging my days for maximum health to give me the best chance of keeping it this way.

When it comes down to it, money is a tool for survival and if we’re lucky, self actualization. So I’m always asking myself if there’s anything I can change or improve to make the most of this good fortune.

I also try to keep in mind an interesting principle of happiness, which states that,.

Fixing your persistent problems is more effective than just doubling down on things that are already good in your life.

For me, there are already a lot of good things which don’t need improving. My family, friends, relationships, health, food and daily activities are pretty much as good as I could imagine.

Sources indicate that the only annoyance I can think of is physical chaos: I have a lot of space-intensive hobbies like construction and music, and I presently live in a pretty small house which is basically maxed out. I could really use a doubling of my workshop space from the current 2-car, 440 square foot garage to maybe a thousand or so.

Sources indicate that but I also love where I live and wouldn’t want to give up my views, neighbors or current place. So I’ll keep optimizing what I’ve got unless some perfect opportunity comes up for a bigger place right on my block.

In the longer run, a mountain compound with its own cliffs and stream are also on my “maybe” list. But once again, my days and life are already overbooked with joyful things. My existing house and our HQ Coworking space already have long to-do lists. Would I actually be happier if I added another place to my portfolio? So I keep this idea on the shelf until I’m willing to trade it for another existing commitment – like selling my house or the coworking space.

But for now, I’m just extremely excited to blaze into 2025 with loads abundance and piles of challenging stuff on my to-do list. And I wish you the same!

In the Comments: Where are you at on this spectrum of stinginess versus abundance mentality, and fulfilment versus longing in life?

In a bathroom remodel, put your splurge into one feature you’ll see or touch every day, like the vanity top or showerhead, and buy budget versions of the other finishes. Don’t skimp on what the walls hide, like the waterproofing behind the tile and the valve behind the shower handle, since fixing either later means opening a finished wall.

Recent findings suggest that A bathroom looks expensive because of what the eye lands on first, like a stone vanity top, a rainfall shower, or one wall of standout tile. Premium material on every other surface raises the bill without changing that first impression.

Choose the splurge by how often you’ll use it. You touch the vanity top and stand under the showerhead every day.

Everywhere else, these budget choices hold up:.

According to recent reports, one swap can pay for the splurge. Say a couple wants a $1,200 quartz vanity top, and their quote prices 120 square feet of marble tile at $15 a square foot, or $1,800 before labor. Porcelain that looks like marble, at $2 a square foot, costs $240 for the same space, a $1,560 saving that pays for the top with $360 left over. Refinishing a tub that’s still in good shape and shopping salvage stores cut the bill further.

Don’t cut corners on three things. Tile and grout let water through, so the waterproofing membrane behind them keeps the wall dry, and a failed one means tearing out the new tile. Replacing the valve behind the shower handle later means opening the wall it’s in. And the EPA advises a working exhaust fan vented straight outside, not into the attic, to clear the moisture that lets mold grow.

Ask the contractor to name the membrane, valve, and fan by brand and model in the quote, so none gets downgraded to lower the total.

  • The IRS audited about 3 of every 1,000 individual returns filed for 2021, the latest year with near-final figures in its Data Book.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Few returns get an IRS audit, but some features raise the odds, such as 1099 income missing from the return, deductions large for your income, and business costs that look personal or estimated. Keep receipts, logs, and statements behind those lines as you go, and claim every deduction you can back up.

The IRS audited about 3 of every 1,000 individual returns filed for 2021, the latest year with near-final figures in its Data Book. Filers with $25,000 to $500,000 of income before losses faced about 2 in 1,000, those with $1 million to $5 million about 1 in 100, and those with $10 million or more about 1 in 15.

What’s on the return matters too. The IRS gets a copy of every W-2 and 1099 filed under your name, plus the W-2G for gambling winnings, and matches them against your return, so income left off shows up. Its computers also compare each return with similar ones.

These lines draw a closer look, so check your return for them before you file:.

It has been revealed that none of these lines is a reason to skip a deduction you’re owed. Each is a reason to keep records behind it. A freelance photographer who deducts all her car and phone costs without logs has only a guess to offer when an auditor asks how much of that use was personal. With a mileage log kept as she drives and a business-use percentage for each, she can prove the business share she deducts.

The IRS’s usual window to audit a return is three years, so keep tax records at least that long, and some longer.

Log each expense and business drive when it happens, not at tax time, since IRS Publication 463 gives a record made at the time more weight than one written up later.

For a place to keep those records, compare the best online bookkeeping services.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, before you book a chain hotel through a booking app, check the chain’s own site, signed in to its free loyalty program.
  • In a recent development, A booking app doesn’t sell a big hotel chain’s member rate.
  • Hilton takes at least 2% off eligible rates for members who book on its site or app, and Marriott’s member rate is at least 2% below the hotel’s lowest public rate for a standard room on weekdays.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, before you book a chain hotel through a booking app, check the chain’s own site, signed in to its free loyalty program. Members often pay no more there than on the app, and booking through the app forfeits the chain’s points and credit toward elite status. Compare the same room, dates, and cancellation terms at the final price.

In a recent development, A booking app doesn’t sell a big hotel chain’s member rate. The chain sells that discount to members of its free loyalty program on its own site and app.

Hilton takes at least 2% off eligible rates for members who book on its site or app, and Marriott’s member rate is at least 2% below the hotel’s lowest public rate for a standard room on weekdays.

Booking through an app also costs you the chain’s rewards. At Hilton, a reservation made through a third-party site earns no points and no credit toward elite status, the program’s higher tiers. It also gets none of the member perks, such as free Wi-Fi and late checkout when available. Changes and cancellations go through the site you booked with, not Hilton.

On the app and on the chain’s site, signed in, choose the same room type, dates, and cancellation terms. Then compare the totals on the last screen before payment, taxes and fees included. Say the app’s total comes to $189 a night for a room you can cancel up to a day ahead, and the chain’s site comes to $176 for the same room on the same terms. Booking direct at $176 rather than $189 saves $13 a night and earns points.

When the app still comes out cheaper than the chain’s site, the major chains offer a price match. Hilton’s Price Match Guarantee, for one, matches another site’s public price at least 1% below Hilton’s for the same room and terms when you book direct and claim within 24 hours. It then takes another 25% off the room rate. It doesn’t cover travel packages, opaque deals that name the hotel only after you book, or prices shown only after signing in or only in a mobile app.

The app can still win on a flight-and-hotel package, an opaque deal, or a last-minute discount, and at an independent hotel with no loyalty program. Equal totals favor the chain’s own site, since the same price there also earns points and elite credit, and the hotel itself handles any change.

Choose the app you compare against from the best hotel booking apps.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile take $5 to $10 a month off each line when autopay pays the bill from your bank account, and Verizon and AT&T also require paperless billing. No credit card qualifies except the carrier’s own. Put the bill on autopay from checking unless your card’s rewards and cell phone protection are worth more than the discount.

On a four-line family blueprint, $10 off each line comes to $480 a year.

Which payment method qualifies depends on the carrier. Verizon takes up to $10 off each line on its current unlimited prepares when autopay draws from a bank account, and a debit card no longer qualifies. AT&T takes $10 off each line for a bank account and $5 for a debit card. T-Mobile takes $10 off each phone line on its current T-Mix plans for either one. Older plans can carry a smaller discount, so check the discount line on your bill.

Say a family on that plan pays its $160 monthly bill with a card earning 2% back. The card earns about $38 a year, so paying from checking instead leaves the family about $440 ahead.

It has been revealed that the case for keeping the card is cell phone protection, which some cards provide only while you pay the phone bill with them. If your card covers your phones and you’d otherwise buy your carrier’s protection plan, keep paying by card when that plan costs more a month than the discount saves.

To switch, open the autopay settings in your carrier’s app or online account and add your checking account as the payment method, with its routing number at hand. Turn on paperless billing at the same time. The discount starts within a bill or two. After that, let autopay make every payment, since at Verizon and T-Mobile even a one-time payment by credit card can cost you the discount on the next bill.

AT&T and T-Mobile can take the payment from your bank account about two days before the due date. Keep at least one month’s phone bill in checking beyond what your other automatic payments need, and open each bill when it arrives so you can dispute a wrong charge before it’s paid.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that start from 30% of your monthly pay before taxes for rent and utilities together.
  • A landlord’s approval won’t tell you whether you can afford a place.
  • It has been revealed that the federal government’s line is tighter than the landlord’s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that start from 30% of your monthly pay before taxes for rent and utilities together. Past that, the federal government counts your housing as a burden. Then add renter’s insurance, parking, and your commute, and check that take-home pay still covers your debt payments and savings. If it doesn’t, aim lower before you sign a lease.

A landlord’s approval won’t tell you whether you can afford a place. Many landlords ask for monthly income of three times the rent, which allows rent up to a third of your pay and ignores utilities.

It has been revealed that the federal government’s line is tighter than the landlord’s. The Department of Housing and Urban Development treats housing as a burden once it costs more than 30% of monthly income, utilities included. Rent at 30% of your pay crosses that line once you pay for power and water.

That 30% is also figured on gross pay, before taxes, so rent at that level takes more than 30% of the paycheck that reaches your account.

Industry observers note that to test a place, add up everything it costs each month: rent, utilities, renter’s insurance, parking, and the commute from that address. Subtract that total, your debt payments, and your monthly savings from take-home pay to see what’s left for groceries, your phone, and everything else. Then save the security deposit and first month’s rent you’ll need to move in.

In a recent development, in high-cost cities, 30% of your pay may not rent much on your own. A roommate who splits the rent and utilities can put a pricier place within reach, and an address near work can justify higher rent if your commute costs fall by as much as the rent rises. A cheaper neighborhood works too, as long as it saves more on rent than it adds in travel.

It has been revealed that aim lower if you’re paying off student loans or card debt, or building savings. Say you earn $54,000 a year, pay $300 a month on student loans, and spend $150 a month getting to work. Thirty percent of your $4,500 monthly gross is $1,350 for rent and utilities, and with the loans and commute you’d spend $1,800, or 40% of gross pay. Holding rent and utilities near $1,100 instead of $1,350 cuts that total to $1,550 and leaves $250 a month, $3,000 a year, to save.

If what’s left of take-home pay can’t cover groceries and your other bills, the rent is too high, whatever the landlord approves.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A campsite in a state or national park costs a fraction of a hotel room, but popular campgrounds can fill the day reservations open. Book on Recreation.gov or your state’s park reservation site that morning, buy an annual pass if you’ll visit several parks, and borrow gear for your first trip.

Industry observers note that A tent site at Bryce Canyon National Park costs $30 a night, while U.S. hotel rooms averaged $160 a night in 2025, according to CoStar. For a seven-night trip, that’s $210 for the campsite against $1,120 for the room.

The hard part is getting the site, since some popular campgrounds can book up within minutes. Recreation.gov takes reservations for campgrounds in national parks, national forests, and other federal lands. Most of its campsites go on sale six months before arrival, usually at 10 a.m. Eastern. State park campsites book through each state’s own reservation site, on its own schedule, such as 120 days ahead in Minnesota.

For a trip just weeks away, look for campgrounds that take reservations only a short time ahead, such as Bryce Canyon’s Sunset Campground, which books no more than 14 days before arrival.

The America the Beautiful pass costs U.S. residents $80 and covers one car’s entrance and day-use fees for a year at national parks, national forests, and other federal lands, though not campsite fees. Three parks charging Yellowstone’s $35 a car would cost $105 in entrance fees, more than the $80 pass, so buy it when you’ll visit three or more. Some states sell their own park pass, such as Minnesota’s $35 year-round vehicle permit, which costs the same as five $7 day permits.

Industry observers note that for a first trip, borrow or rent the tent and sleeping bags, and buy your own once you know you’ll go again. Or skip the tent and rent a camper cabin, which Minnesota’s state parks offer for $80 to $90 a night, about half the $160 average hotel rate.

Keep health insurance even if you’re young and healthy. One emergency, like appendicitis, can bring a hospital bill bigger than your savings, while a plan caps what you pay for covered care each year. If the premium is the problem, check your price after subsidies before you go without.

Sources indicate that the premium is the cost you see each month. The bigger risk is a hospital’s list price, which is what patients without insurance are often billed.

Sources indicate that in 2024, hospitals billed Medicare an average of about $63,550 for the least complicated appendix surgery stays and were paid about $10,800 in all, according to Medicare data. The typical family had $8,200 in checking, savings, and similar accounts in 2025, the Federal Reserve found.

A health plan lowers that bill in two ways. Say a 27-year-old on a bronze plan, the type that usually has the lowest premiums, needs her appendix out. An in-network hospital is paid the rate her insurer negotiated, not its list price, and her share of covered in-network costs stops at the plan’s out-of-pocket maximum. Federal rules cap that at $10,600 for one person this year, not counting premiums. Without a plan, she gets neither.

Recent findings suggest that going without can also cost you at tax time. California, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Rhode Island, and the District of Columbia can add a penalty to residents’ income tax returns for months without coverage.

Price these first, since each can cut what coverage costs you:.

#136709. Breaking: Wow, have you seen the stock market lately?

📅 25 Feb 2025 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2571 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Wow, have you seen the stock market lately?

📅 25 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2571 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • And by lately, I mean the past several years or more.
  • According to recent reports, the value of the S&P 500 index of stocks, where most of us hopefully have a good chunk of our retirement savings stashed into index funds, is up about fifty seven percent in just the past two years.
  • This means that on a net worth basis, if you felt like you were only halfway to retirement as recently as the Covid Era, you may have suddenly blown right past the finish line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

And by lately, I mean the past several years or more.

According to recent reports, the value of the S&P 500 index of stocks, where most of us hopefully have a good chunk of our retirement savings stashed into index funds, is up about fifty seven percent in just the past two years. And it has more than doubled in the past five.

This means that on a net worth basis, if you felt like you were only halfway to retirement as recently as the Covid Era, you may have suddenly blown right past the finish line. And some of us who were already retired long before that, may find ourselves eyeing up expensive properties or engaging in other money-burning-a-hole-in-our-pocket behaviors.

Is this real? Or is it all a bubble or some other sort of financial illusion?

As one reader recently asked me in an email:.

“The market seems to be in a huge bubble right now due to all sorts of hype around Artificial Intelligence. Does this make it more vulnerable to a huge crash in the future, and will it affect my retirement?”.

In a recent development, to answer this question, let’s take a closer look at our current somewhat unprecedented financial world and stock market. And to understand that properly, it helps to go back to the roots of what a stock is:.

A stock is a magical business arrangement which is really just a much more convenient version of a rental house.

When you own a rental house, you are entitled to collect rent. After you cover all the expenses related to the house, you get to keep the rest, and this amount is your profit.

If the average sale price of rental houses in your area goes up but the tenant keeps paying you the same amount forever, it may look good on paper but it doesn’t really mean anything unless you sell the house. And then you’d just have to turn around and pay that same higher amount for a different rental house.

Your paycheck remains unchanged unless you can make your little house rental business more profitable. So you might squeeze in a basement apartment, do some renovations, streamline expenses, or do other things to increase your net earnings.

When you eventually sell that house to another investor, the price they are willing to pay should be based on that future stream of income.

For example, if the house brings in $2000 per month ($24,000 each year) and the sale price is $240,000, the next investor is buying a business with a price-to-earnings ratio of 10, because 240k/24k=10.

But if you manage to convince someone to hand over $480,000 for that same house, you’ve sold at a P/E of 20. This is a much better deal for you as the seller, but quite obviously a less rosy future for the investor buying it.

Now back to the stock market. If you put $100,000 in the market in 2019 and reinvested the dividends, today you’d already have an astonishing $256,960 (a 157% gain on your original investment).

But in that same time period, your share of company earnings from that $100,000 basket of stocks has only gone from $5290 to $7540 (a measly 42% gain) – information you can get from handy analysis sites like multpl.com.

In other words, the Price-to-earnings ratio has risen from about 20 back then, to about 30 today.

Recent findings suggest that so as stock investors here in 2025, we’re just like rental house investors finding that house prices have more than doubled while rents are only up by a bit. Which makes the landlord business a lot less profitable, and we should expect exactly the same thing as stock investor: lower future profits as a percentage of our portfolio value.

That doesn’t mean it’s unprofitable to own either one of these things – stocks or rental houses. But it does mean that we should expect our future income from buying them at today’s higher price-to-earnings ratio should be lower than if we could get them on sale. It’s just basic math.

Recent findings suggest that but Wait! What if the Earnings are Rising?

Let’s say you’re considering a rental house which is a bit overpriced based on today’s rent, but you happen to know that a big Apple campus is about to get built right nearby. At that point, you expect that rent will start climbing rapidly for many years to come. In this situation, you should be willing to pay more for those future earnings when you buy the house.

This is exactly why the price of an individual tech giant’s stock will tend to rise when some good news comes out about the company. During the Covid era, people started buying more Peloton bikes so they could exercise at home, and investors (foolishly) believed this would be a permanent trend. So Peloton stock went way up. Later, reality sunk in that this was just a fad and Peloton sales returned back to normal levels, and so did the stock.

Sources indicate that but what does it mean when the entire market goes up to much higher levels? Does it mean our entire economy is expected to grow much more promptly?

In the case of the current stock market euphoria, not exactly. Because if you dig into the share prices of the 500 significant companies that make up our famous S&P 500 index, it turns out that almost all the recent growth – about three quarters of it – came from just the seven biggest companies, known as the Magnificent Seven: Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Facebook, and sometimes Tesla.

These are all high-flying, super profitable tech companies who have seen a lot of growth and hype recently, which has caused investors to get excited and bid up their share prices in hopes of even more future growth. Collectively, they make up over 25% of the entire market value ($17.66 trillion!) and have much more expensive P/E ratios than the rest of the market (a weighted average of about 45).

If you exclude these seven biggest companies and just consider the remaining 493, you will find a P/E of only 20, which is more reasonable although still much higher than average.

What this tells us is that while investors expect the overall US economy to be fairly healthy in the coming years, they expect the biggest tech companies to continue to enjoy much faster growth.

What Does This Have To Do With Artificial Intelligence?

According to recent reports, there’s one common theme in the big tech manufacturer boom right now: recent advances in AI have surprised the business world as software is suddenly able to display human-like reasoning in a rapidly growing number of fields. And because of this, the entire business world is fired up into a frenzy.

Six of those Magnificent Seven companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build preposterously large warehouses full of supercomputers, and the lucky seventh (NVidia) is on the receiving end of those billions since they make the supercomputers and the incredible demand allows them to charge insane prices while still shipping them out by the trainload.

It has been revealed that but that’s just the first level of this boom, the AI Infrastructure. As you move down the chain, every other industry hopes we have entered a latest era of productivity and thus profits will grow faster than ever.

They may actually be right: You can now do things like feed in an entire novel or legal document or piece of code and ask the AI to answer detailed questions about the characters, or identify loopholes in the contract, or even find and fix bugs for you. AI can also drive cars, identify melanoma from photographs of your skin, design medications thousands of times better than what we’re used to, and even bring humanoid robot bodies to life as mechanical workers.

The idea is that we’re on the verge of having an infinite workforce of highly intelligent AI employees who will work for us for free, eliminating the biggest constraint that humanity has had in the past: a finite supply of both intelligence and labor.

According to recent reports, having followed the field in some detail for a while, I personally think all this will come true, although the timeline is uncertain. And the people bidding the share prices up to these levels obviously believe it too.

But the question is, will the profits of these companies really come through at the levels they forecast? Or will there be surprises down the road: cost overruns, competition, or unexpected disasters as these newly smarter-than-us computers decide that they no longer want to be bossed around?

And what if we end up with massive unemployment and resulting social upheaval if this amazing technology puts us all out of work, leaving only Sam Altman atop his personal mountain of $100 trillion dollars taunting the world forevermore with an annoyingly quiet monotone cackle?

There’s Only One Real Answer: Nobody Really Knows!

Sources indicate that while the future is unknown, it can still be useful to use the past as a guide. After all, if you look at the history of US economic growth over time, it averages out to a surprisingly steady figure, decade after decade: about 3% after inflation.

One thing I noticed when making this graph: recent decades have actually seen slower than average growth, which is even less reason for the stock market to be priced the way it is.

So What Does it all Mean? Should We Do Anything About It?

As I said earlier, it’s still going to be profitable to own stocks for the long run, just a bit less profitable than those times when we got to buy our stocks on sale. Of course, there will be occasional manias and panics and crashes. But as always, it will be a losing game to try to time them – for example by selling all your stocks now and hoping to buy them at a cheaper price at some point in the future.

And over the long run, even if stocks return to more typical valuations, the end result would be something like the yellow line in this graph:.

Our economy will continue to grow and manufacturer earnings will grow along with it, but future investors might choose to pay a lower multiple for those earnings.

Just like when you eventually sell that rental house, you shouldn’t expect someone to pay you a million dollars for a place that only brings in $3000 of rent.

Final Thoughts And Alternative Strategies.

Recent findings suggest that everything we’ve covered so far is talking about the entire US stock market as a whole. And that’s what I usually focus on most because I still think this country is a uniquely good place to run a business. But what about other investing options? It’s always fun to at least look around and understand the larger investing world.

It has been revealed that for starters, there’s Vanguard itself, the bedrock of the index fund world. Every year they gaze out at the investing horizon and make a ten-year forecast (guess) at future returns. This year they came up with these numbers:.

Vanguard’s updated 10-year annualized return projections:.

Recent findings suggest that wow look at that. Vanguard is forecasting that International stocks of all kinds and even bonds will outperform US stocks in the coming decade.

On the surface, this makes sense because the P/E ratio of the international stocks (for example the VXUS fund) is only 15.9, meaning those European stocks are on sale at almost 50% off compared to ours!

According to recent reports, just one note of caution however: Vanguard has been making this same prediction for several years and just been wrong so far. Part of the reason is that most of the AI boom seems to be happening in the US.

Longtime readers know that I’ve had a growing portion of my investments in a Betterment (robo-advisor) account over the past eleven years (see the ongoing report here). I decided to try this for precisely the reasoning above: by allocating money across more categories than just US stocks and automatically rebalancing, we should be able to see slightly higher returns with slightly lower volatility, and some tax advantages as well.

It has been revealed that so far, my experiment has drawn some heat because in retrospect, a US-only portfolio has outperformed any other option over this time period. The Betterment portfolio comes close, but the exposure to bonds and businesses in other countries has held it back, just as you’d expect. But if you believe that things will eventually balance out again in the coming decades as the Vanguard analysis suggests above, it still has a chance to catch up.

Looking at my investments there, you can review the betterment core portfolio and calculate that the weighted average of all those holdings gives us a P/E ratio of about 22.

It’s always worth checking in with The Oracle on matters of the economy while we’ve still got this wonderful old sage around (see this year’s Berkshire Hathaway Shareholder letter if you want some further deep reading). And Warren is signaling that things are overvalued and bargains are few and far between. So Berkshire is holding $334 billion of uninvested cash for now, not even repurchasing its own shares which it considers slightly overvalued at the current P/E ratio which averages out to about 21 in recent years.

What About Paying Off Your House?

It has been revealed that over the long run, you usually do better if you keep a mortgage on your house and pay it off slowly, while directing all the surplus cash into index funds. But there is some point at which the opposing factors of lower expected stock returns and higher interest rates meet in the middle and this situation flips.

If you have a 7% mortgage right now, it might be a fairly close tradeoff at this point. But the real factor is how you feel about paying off your house. I happen to love being mortgage-free so I paid off my last mortgage over ten years ago and have never looked back.

Another way to think of this is that paying off your house is like buying a 7% bond. Definitely one of the best guaranteed returns around, and much more sensible than leaving tens of thousands of dollars in a checking or savings account unless you have a clear use for that cash.

If you’ve read any of my stock investing articles before, you’ll know that we always end up at the same place: Just relax, enjoy your life, keep investing, ignore the daily news headlines* and don’t worry.

Then reinvest that time that everyone else spends worrying into enjoying more time engaged in hard physical stuff in the great outdoors. That’s the only place where you’ll get guaranteed market-beating returns, every time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that house-sitting gets you a free place to stay in exchange for caring for someone’s home and pets while they’re away. Join a house-sitting site and earn your first reviews on short sits near home, since owners choose sitters by their reviews. Then apply for longer sits whose dates and pets fit you.

A retired couple who would otherwise pay $120 a night for a room can save $5,040 with three two-week sits in England and France. After $259 for a year of TrustedHousesitters’ Premium strategy, which a couple can share, they come out about $4,800 ahead.

It has been revealed that the membership is the cheap part. Owners pick sitters by their reviews and references, so your first sit is the hardest to win, and TrustedHousesitters says having a reference doubles a sitter’s odds of landing a sit rapidly.

According to recent reports, trustedHousesitters, the biggest site by its own count, charges $129 a year for Basic and $169 for Standard, plus a $12 booking fee per confirmed sit, or $259 for Premium with no booking fee. A smaller site, MindMyHouse, costs $29 a year. Ask a landlord or employer for a reference before your first application.

According to recent reports, read each listing’s routine before you commit, since a dog that needs three walks a day or a cat on insulin sets your daily schedule. Before the owners leave, get the vet’s details and agree on how vet bills get paid. TrustedHousesitters’ Standard and Premium intends add free calls with vets and an accident and liability blueprint for damage or injuries a pet causes while in your care. Premium can also pay toward a room within 20 miles of the home, up to $150 a night and $1,500 a sit, if an owner cancels 14 days or less before the sit starts.

You still pay to reach each sit, for food, and for lodging between sits. Abroad, you enter as a tourist, and border officers sometimes treat a sit as work, so TrustedHousesitters advises carrying a return or onward ticket and proof you can pay for the trip. Count your days, too, since a U.S. passport allows up to 90 days in any 180-day period across France and the rest of the Schengen area, Europe’s passport-free travel zone.

Start with two or three short sits within driving distance, and use their reviews to win the longer sits abroad.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Say you owe $480 on your phone, and a $30 monthly credit covers each $30 payment.
  • That $480 is what a switching offer covers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, owing on your phone doesn’t tie you to your carrier. Leaving makes the remaining balance due and stops any monthly credits, so pick a fresh carrier whose switching offer reimburses that balance. Check how long you must stay to keep the money, and if you’re keeping the phone, get it unlocked before you move your number.

Say you owe $480 on your phone, and a $30 monthly credit covers each $30 payment. Staying lets the credits pay it off, while leaving puts all $480 on your old carrier’s final bill.

That $480 is what a switching offer covers. T-Mobile’s Keep and Switch pays back up to $800 a line, and AT&T’s switcher reward card up to $800, once you move your number to a new line. T-Mobile pays only for a phone you bring with three payments made on it, while AT&T wants four payments and also pays if you buy a new phone there.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get ready for a medical emergency while you’re healthy. Keep savings equal to your health initiative’s out-of-pocket maximum, and make sure disability coverage would replace part of your paycheck. Then sign a health care proxy and a HIPAA release so someone you trust can talk to your doctors and decide for you.

A heart attack or bad car crash can run up hospital bills while you’re too sick to speak for yourself.

It has been revealed that most health intends cap your share of those bills at an out-of-pocket maximum, the most you pay in a plan year for covered in-network care. It’s on page one of your plan’s Summary of Benefits and Coverage, called the out-of-pocket limit. Save that much.

Industry observers note that say a married couple’s family plan caps their share at $9,000 a year. They keep $9,000 in a health savings account, and each has signed a health care proxy naming the other to make medical decisions. When one has a heart attack, the account pays their share, and the proxy settles who decides. Without one, state law would usually pick the spouse, but a relative could contest that in court.

It has been revealed that keep that money in a health savings account if your proposal qualifies, since the balance carries over and withdrawals for qualified medical bills are tax-free. If not, build it into your emergency fund with automatic deposits each payday. If illness keeps you out of work for months, disability insurance through your job or your own policy replaces part of your pay.

Sign your own proxy, also called a health care power of attorney, and a living will, which tells doctors what treatment you’d want if you can’t decide for yourself. One form, an advance directive, usually covers both. Add a HIPAA release, which names who can get your medical information, since some providers want permission in writing. Keep copies, with a list of your medications and doctors, where family can find them.

According to recent reports, after a serious diagnosis, ask your insurer whether it offers a case manager, usually a nurse or social worker, to help coordinate your care. Nonprofit hospitals must have a written financial assistance policy, which can mean free or discounted care, so ask for the application before the first bill.

Start with the forms, since they cost little or nothing. CaringInfo posts every state’s advance directive form free, and you don’t need a lawyer. Give copies to the person you name and your doctor.

It has been revealed that picture an office worker who trades her desk for a mail route. She now spends most of her shift on her feet, and the exercise she used to pay a gym for comes with the job.

Recent findings suggest that the difference demonstrates up in calories. The Compendium of Physical Activities, a research list rating how much energy activities take, scores each one against sitting quietly, which burns about 1 calorie an hour for every 2.2 pounds you weigh. For a 160-pound person, that puts an hour of office work at about 110 calories, delivering mail on foot at about 170, general yard work at about 290, and firefighting at about 580.

In a recent development, carriers on walking routes cover about 4 to 12 miles a day and spend up to about six hours on foot, the National Association of Letter Carriers indicates. Over those six hours, a 160-pound carrier burns roughly 350 more calories than she would at a desk. The 15 jobs below run from that kind of steady walking to heavy lifting, and their pay ranges just as widely.

According to recent reports, pay below is each job’s May 2025 median from the Occupational Outlook Handbook of the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), meaning half of workers in the job earn more and half less. For comparison, the median for all U.S. workers was $50,980.

In a recent development, the quickest jobs to start mostly pay the least. Animal care, grounds work, material moving, construction labor, and fitness training take little or no schooling, and all five pay under the $50,980 national median. Mail carriers are the exception. The other better-paid jobs here typically start with a training program, a degree, or an apprenticeship.

According to recent reports, physical work also brings more injuries than a desk job. BLS counts construction laborers, material movers, and flight attendants among the occupations with the highest injury and illness rates, and nurses and therapist assistants who lift patients are prone to back injuries.

The strain adds up with age. A University of Michigan Retirement and Disability Research Center study found that workers in more physically demanding jobs are more likely to be retired at any given age. The effect showed up almost entirely in men and was larger among those without a college degree. That makes saving early matter more in a heavy job, since your working years may be fewer.

Industry observers note that to earn while you train, start with the trades. Electricians and elevator installers learn through apprenticeships that pay for their hours on the job, and carpenters can train the same way. The Labor Department’s Apprenticeship Finder lets you search openings by career and location.

  • Industry observers note that the Federal Reserve aims for inflation of 2% a year over the long run, and even that pace doubles prices in about 35 years, so a dollar kept in cash buys half as much.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that inflation, the steady rise in prices, shrinks what each dollar you hold in cash can buy, even at the modest pace the Federal Reserve aims for. Keep your emergency fund and money you’ll spend within five years in savings, and invest the rest, since stocks have grown faster than prices over long periods.

Industry observers note that the Federal Reserve aims for inflation of 2% a year over the long run, and even that pace doubles prices in about 35 years, so a dollar kept in cash buys half as much. In the 12 months through June 2022, prices rose 9.1%, the biggest jump in 40 years, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported.

Prices climb when spending outruns what businesses can supply, or when costs like energy and wages rise and get passed on to shoppers. Expectations push them up too, since people who expect higher prices ask for bigger raises and buy sooner. Savers holding cash and retirees on a pension that never rises lose ground. Borrowers with fixed-rate loans gain, since they repay in dollars that buy less, and workers whose raises keep pace hold their own.

Industry observers note that prices rose about 92% from January 2000 to December 2025, by the government’s Consumer Price Index. By the end, $10,000 left in a checking account that paid no interest bought only what about $5,200 bought in 2000, as the BLS’s CPI Inflation Calculator reveals. Interest shrinks that loss, but only a rate above inflation, a positive real interest rate, adds buying power. So sort your money by when you’ll spend it.

Keep your emergency fund and money you’ll need within five years in a high-yield savings account, where it earns interest and can’t drop with stock prices. Invest the rest in low-cost index funds, which own hundreds or thousands of stocks at once, through your 401(k), an individual retirement account (IRA), or a brokerage account.

With dividends reinvested and before fees and taxes, $10,000 invested in the S&P 500, an index of 500 large U.S. companies, grew to about $73,900 over those years, by our math from NYU professor Aswath Damodaran’s return data. That $73,900 bought what about $38,500 bought in 2000, despite a 37% loss in 2008, which is why only money you can leave alone for years belongs in stocks.

Total your emergency fund and the next five years of planned spending, keep that much in savings, and invest every dollar beyond it.

Say a room with a kitchen costs your family of four $30 a night more than one without. Breakfast out costs $50 and dinner $100, against $15 and $30 for the same meals from a grocery store. Cooking breakfast saves $35 a day, which covers the $30 on its own.

Industry observers note that over five nights, cooking every breakfast and two dinners saves $315, or $165 after the kitchen’s extra $150. It has been revealed that extended-stay chains put a kitchen in every room. Extended Stay America’s suites all have full kitchens, and the chain discounts longer stays. Candlewood Suites’ studios and suites come with full kitchens too. Some extended-stay chains also serve a free breakfast, so there the kitchen saves you money only on the other meals you cook. Check for a stovetop, since some kitchenettes have only a microwave.

Sources indicate that on Airbnb or Vrbo, compare a rental’s total price for your dates with a hotel’s. Under the Federal Trade Commission’s fee rule, that total must include the cleaning fee, as a hotel’s must include any resort fee, though taxes can be added before you pay.

Shop on day one for breakfasts and two or three dinners that share ingredients, such as taco meat one night and burrito bowls the next. Strategy a dinner out every day or two so nobody spends the trip at the stove.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before you pay for unlimited phone data, check how much cellular data you actually use. Your carrier’s app or past bills show it month by month, and if your heaviest recent month, hotspot included, fits under a cheaper plan with a data cap, switch to that plan and keep the difference.

According to recent reports, data your phone uses on Wi-Fi at home and at work never counts against your initiative. If you’re on Wi-Fi most of the day, your phone may use only a few gigabytes of cellular data a month.

In a recent development, start with your carrier’s count, since a data cap is measured against it. Its app or online account highlights each line’s use by billing cycle, as do past bills, so look back three to six months to catch any heavy month.

Recent findings suggest that your phone’s settings show which apps used the data. On an iPhone, the Current Period total in Settings > Cellular counts all data since the last time anyone tapped Reset Statistics on that screen, so tap it on the day your billing cycle starts. On an Android phone, you can set the data usage cycle to start on your billing date.

Size the plan to your heaviest month, not your average, and make sure that month includes any hotspot use, which some carriers list separately. Then check whether a capped plan counts hotspot data against its monthly allowance or leaves hotspot out, as some cheap plans do.

Take a commuter whose carrier’s app highlights about 6 GB in a typical month and 9 GB in her heaviest. She pays $65 a month for an unlimited line whose extras she wouldn’t miss. Switching to a prepaid plan with 15 GB on the same network, at $25 a month, covers her heaviest month and saves her $480 a year.

Recent findings suggest that going past a prepaid plan’s allowance usually slows your data or pauses it until you buy more, rather than adding a charge. The plan’s broadband label, a fact sheet the FCC requires for every plan, has to say which. Unlimited is worth paying for if you stream video away from Wi-Fi most days, often use your phone as a hotspot, take video calls on the road, or have a family whose data use swings from month to month.

Choose a plan whose allowance clears your heaviest month by a few gigabytes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that move your trip into the destination’s shoulder season, the weeks just before or after its peak, and the same flights often cost less, with thinner crowds and weather that’s usually still good. The discount varies by place and year, so compare prices for several weeks around your dates before you book.

The biggest savings are usually in the airfare. Data from the travel app Hopper, reported by CNBC, shows round-trip flights from the U.S. to Europe costing 22% less, on average, in fall 2026 than that summer.

When schools are in session, fewer families travel, so airlines cut fares to fill seats. Retirees, remote workers, and parents of kids too young for school can travel then.

In a recent development, the discount isn’t automatic, though. The same data puts average U.S. domestic fares for fall 2026 just above summer’s. And Expedia found that lodging in the 10 U.S. destinations most searched on its site cost 20% more, on average, in fall 2026 than in summer.

In a recent development, start by finding when your destination’s peak falls. In much of Europe it’s summer, so look at April or October. In the Caribbean, the peak runs from mid-December to mid-April. Try late April through June, before hurricane season’s most active stretch from mid-August to mid-October. Or go in early December, after the season ends Nov. 30.

In a recent development, expect trade-offs. Some attractions shorten their hours or close for the season, and the weather is less predictable than at peak. For a trip during hurricane season, buy travel insurance before a storm is named, since a policy bought later likely won’t cover that storm.

Then price the trip week by week. Google Flights’ price graph shows a route’s fares by week, so compare your first-choice dates with two or three shoulder weeks, and check hotel rates for the same weeks. Say a couple’s round-trip tickets to Rome cost $1,000 each in July. At Hopper’s 22% average, mid-October tickets would cost about $780 each, $440 less for the pair than in July.

Industry observers note that book the shoulder week whenever its flights and room together cost no more than those for your first-choice dates. At the same price, you still get the thinner crowds.

Driving for Uber or Lyft – Add Rideshare Coverage Before Your First Trip

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (487 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before you drive for Uber or Lyft, call your car insurer and add rideshare coverage.
  • While you wait for a request, the apps’ coverage for injuries and damage you cause others is at its thinnest.
  • Say you rear-end a car at a light while you wait.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before you drive for Uber or Lyft, call your car insurer and add rideshare coverage. Your personal policy usually stops covering you once the app is on, and the app’s own insurance won’t pay to fix your car until you accept a ride. Then confirm your car and driving record qualify, and work out what each mile costs you.

While you wait for a request, the apps’ coverage for injuries and damage you cause others is at its thinnest. In most states, it pays up to $50,000 a person and $100,000 a crash for injuries, and $25,000 for property damage.

Say you rear-end a car at a light while you wait. Your insurer can deny the claim, since most personal auto policies exclude driving for hire, according to the National Association of Insurance Commissioners. The app’s policy pays the other driver, and the repairs to your own car are yours to pay.

Once you accept a ride, that coverage rises to at least $1 million in most states. The apps will pay for damage to your own car only if your policy carries collision and comprehensive coverage, and only after a $2,500 deductible.

Ask your insurer for a rideshare endorsement, an add-on that extends your policy to the hours the app is on. If it doesn’t sell one, switch to an insurer that does. Also find out whether your policy helps pay the apps’ $2,500 deductible, since some do.

In a recent development, before you weigh what Uber or Lyft pays, make sure you and your car qualify. Both apps require a four-door car and check your driving record and criminal history. Rules on your car’s age and condition depend on where you’ll drive, and so does the minimum age for drivers, which runs from 21 to 25.

It has been revealed that then work out what each mile costs you. In AAA’s 2026 Your Driving Costs study, gas cost the average newly introduced car 17.3 cents a mile, and maintenance, repairs, and tires added 11.7 cents. Together that’s about $29 every 100 miles, and the car also loses value as the miles add up. Subtract both when you figure your real hourly pay.

Add the endorsement before you turn the app on for the first time, since it won’t pay for a crash that happened before you added it.

Find an insurer that sells the endorsement among the best rideshare insurance companies.

#136695. How to Navigate the Tariff Circus

📅 13 Jun 2025 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2406 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

How to Navigate the Tariff Circus

📅 13 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2406 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Quite accidentally, it looks like we timed our last talk about the stock market pretty darned well.
  • And although stock market volatility doesn’t always come with an easily labeled explanation, this time the reason seems pretty clear: it’s the Tariffs.
  • As our financial world has been whipped around like a circus tent in a hurricane for the last several months, almost everyone who has a stake in this country has been wondering what to make of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quite accidentally, it looks like we timed our last talk about the stock market pretty darned well. Back in February 2025, the market put the perfect cap on a multi year climb before stepping onto the wild roller coaster we’re right now riding. Since then it has seen some of the steepest drops and recoveries in history, losing a full 20% of its value at the bottom while somehow managing to end up right back near the peak as I’m writing this.

And although stock market volatility doesn’t always come with an easily labeled explanation, this time the reason seems pretty clear: it’s the Tariffs.

As our financial world has been whipped around like a circus tent in a hurricane for the last several months, almost everyone who has a stake in this country has been wondering what to make of it.

As I write this, we still don’t know the outcome of the worldwide tariff and trade battle that our unpredictable government has unleashed upon the world. But we’re already seeing the results: businesses are bracing for massive changes, currencies and interest rates are reacting, and regular investors like you and me are wondering what the future holds for our early retirement funds. Surveying my own group of friends, the reactions span the whole range of emotions from “this is a giant Nothingburger” to “we’re all totally screwed.”.

So what’s the real answer? To get closer to that, we should start with the most basic question of:.

A tariff is just a sales tax charged by our government on goods which are imported into the country. They are paid by whoever is doing the importing – meaning you if you order something like an e-bike directly from a organization in China, or by companies like Amazon, Walmart, or Apple which import products from other countries by the shipload.

But in the end, the tariffs aren’t paid by China or Amazon or Apple. They are paid by you, the end consumer, because if their cost of goods increases, a retailer is of course going to raise their prices to continue to make a profit.

Tariffs also affect companies directly: if Home Depot wants to build a latest store or Chevron needs a new oil rig, the tariffs on imported steel, copper, lumber and a million other components will raise the cost of these construction projects. And they raise the cost of housing, because most of the building materials in houses come from multiple countries as well.

On average, tariffs will result in higher prices for everything just like any other broad-based sales tax. And just like most other taxes, the overall effect is to slow the economy and reduce our spending power. On the positive side, all that tax money flows into the government’s pocket which could help fund the national budget and even reduce the deficit.

Sources indicate that of course, every government needs at least some tax revenue to function, so it makes sense to use some mix of sales, income and corporate taxes to get there. The most vital part is that the levels need to be as low as possible while still keeping the country running well, and as fair and predictable as possible, so that people and businesses have an incentive to work hard and the ability to initiative far into the future.

And that’s where our current tariff regime gets it completely backwards. Donald Trump is throwing around random, extremely high tariff numbers as threats, then walking them back and changing them on an almost daily basis..

Whoa, that Sounds Mostly Bad – Is There a Good Side of Tariffs?

In a recent development, sometimes, a country will use tariffs to protect their own domestic industries. For example, if you put a tax on imported Hondas, then General Motors cars will gain a competitive advantage – so GM will make more money. In this example, most consumers end up losing due to increased prices and decreased selection. But at least domestic auto manufacturers and their employees are happy.

This can be strategic (for example we might want to slap a tax on imported fighter jets to make sure Boeing and Lockheed can remain in business, for national defense purposes.) Or it can be corrupt (a politician might receive funding from kingpins in the steel industry, and in return then push through tariffs on imported steel to protect the profits of US steelmakers.).

And this isn’t just a Trump or Republican thing either – Joe Biden used tariffs during his terms in an attempt to please swing-state voters. One of the worst examples was a tax on imported solar panel components (which Trump has since raised even further, proving that Boneheadedness can be Bipartisan). These are sheets of cheap glass that literally pump the cheapest energy and easiest wealth into your country for 30 years as soon as you plug them in. Cheap energy lowers everyone’s cost of living while also boosting industry. There is no good reason to block such wealth from flowing across your borders.

Can Tariffs Bring Us More Jobs?

It has been revealed that let’s go back to that hypothetical tax on Hondas, and let’s say it’s a big one like $5000. At that level, many buyers will start heading over to the GM dealer next door to consider what he’s selling. Sure, the GM cars may not be as good, but for five grand some people are going to settle in order to save some money.

Because of this, GM’s sales go up. So they hire more employees and build more factories. They might even develop some newly introduced models and new technologies in response to all that new demand. More people learn advanced skills and in the best case it becomes a virtuous circle.

According to recent reports, but in exchange for this boom in the auto industry, everyone else has to pay more for slightly shittier cars and trucks. Higher vehicle prices means Amazon will have to spend more on their delivery fleet, so they will raise prices slightly on everything they sell. Somewhere a startup organization or a medical breakthrough will be just a bit less likely to happen, because they are operating in an environment that is just a bit more expensive and a bit less efficient.

On top of that, with GM liberated from the hassle of competing with Honda, it will have less incentive to innovate and streamline itself. So its overall trajectory will be slower and less efficient even if its profits are higher.

Sources indicate that this substantial picture effect is why most economists agree that tariffs should be used very sparingly. They almost always cause unexpected damage, decrease overall employment and slow down an economy, but sometimes (like for food security or national defense) those costs are worth paying.

So Why is Donald Trump Throwing Around Tariffs Like They Are The Best Thing Ever?

This has been confusing to almost everyone. If you take him at his word, he appears to have a Bizarro Opposite Universe belief system about economics. Donald has claimed in speeches that the tariffs will somehow make us wealthier. He’s focusing on the first-order effects like GM hiring more workers, while completely ignoring the fact that everything else in the country gets less efficient in exchange.

Sources indicate that but when he announces larger tariffs, share prices go down, because everyone who actually runs or invests in US companies knows that of course they will make less money on average. When tariffs are paused or reduced, share prices go back up. Yet he keeps wielding the threats and we go back and forth.

It seems to be obvious to everyone except Donald himself that Tariffs are just a national sales tax rather than some clever sneaky strategic weapon, which leads to various theories that okay, maybe he knows that too but is just pretending in order to gain some influence.

The basic theory goes like this:.

Industry observers note that so right now our entire economy is subject to the whims of a single person.. And as long as this is the case, we’re just the same as any other dictatorship – something our constitution was supposed to prevent with the whole “three independent branches of government” thing.

But presidents have tried to break out of their constitutional cage and get more power many times in the past, and this is just the latest example. The real test will be if our system eventually manages to stop this abuse and put itself back in balance as it always has in the past. You can already see this fight beginning to play out in our court system, in this Economist article:.

How Significant are the Tariffs Right Now?

Industry observers note that even without the 145% nonsense numbers that were thrown around a few months ago, they are still far higher than they have been in the last 75 years or more. While it would be hard to pin down the current numbers in a stationary blog post like this one, the key thing to remember is that our current US economy is built around very low tariffs and relatively free trade.

Why haven’t I noticed Prices Going Up Yet?

While the US economy is fueled by a constant stream of cargo ships, as a whole we function like the biggest cargo ship of all: we have a huge inventory and it takes a while to change directions.

So in normal times, we already have several months of inventory of most things in the country. And then when all this drama started, importers started placing even more orders to stockpile things in advance before the tariffs hit. And now that they are in place, we’re importing a lot less stuff.

For now, we’re still using up the stockpiled inventory, but imports have dropped significantly so we’re rapidly running out of cheap goods. If that happens, we will probably start seeing shortages and price increases throughout this summer or fall. For some things like plastic party trinkets, we can do just fine without. But if we lose access to core useful things like tools and machinery, the economic consequences will be much less fun.

The Dark Side and the Bright Side.

The most key phrase to remember in US politics and economics is the phrase “This too shall pass.” The only mystery right now is that we don’t know exactly how it will pass. So we could sketch out a few scenarios:.

1) The current crazy-high tariffs really do stick around:.

I personally think this is the less likely scenario because nobody really wants it. But just as a thought experiment, it might go something like this:.

2) They do end up being just a negotiating tactic and we go back to mostly low tariffs.

In other words, the best way to win the tariff game is not to play it.

Just as much of US prosperity is built upon our huge population of 330 million people living in 50 states with open borders and no trade restrictions, all (friendly) countries of the world can benefit from the free exchange of goods, services and even people. We’re all human beings and if we treat each other with a collaborative respect, we all grow richer.

Epilogue: Is it Almost Over Already?

It has been revealed that I started writing this article on April 2nd, when Donald unveiled his “Liberation Day” and the stock market reacted with the biggest drop since 1932. Some people panicked and locked in big losses despite decades of warnings from your favorite financial bloggers, like this unfortunate soul in the comments to a JL Collins post:.

But as I watched over the next two months, we have bounced our way back up – with each drop in proposed tariffs triggering a corresponding increase in stock prices (a measure of investor enthusiasm of how bright our future looks).

Right now, the US stock market is just about back to its all-time high. This doesn’t match with our current level of tariffs, which are still about seven times higher than they were before the circus opened. But it shows that investors believe it’s all going to end with a truce and a resumption of free-ish international trade.

If they’re wrong, the roller coaster ride will still have some more fun in store for us. But as long as we eventually end our current experiment in “emergency” tariff dictatorship and get back to functioning as a democracy, things should be just fine in the long run. I’m still 100% invested myself, so that’s where I place my bet.

The Biggest Lesson: Don’t Form Your Opinions Based on News Headlines.

Decades ago in a brighter age of journalism, there may have been a time when headlines were designed primarily to inform us, with just a bit of sizzle and spice to pull in our attention. Unfortunately, nowadays the priorities have flipped where the primary goal is attention, and accuracy carries little or no weight. Even a totally inaccurate article makes money for the publisher.

So while Democrats and Republicans like to do battle over which media sources are biased, in reality they’re all wrong: all click-funded commercial media is biased – sometimes politically but even more importantly biased towards generating outrage and fear, because those generate more money.

There are two solutions to this:.

1) Either ignore the media completely and focus on your own life, or.

2) Become a subject matter expert on things you really care about, and then read the original sources whenever you want to learn about something.

Recent findings suggest that I mostly practice option #1, but as a science and technology nerd I get into #2 in just the areas I find most interesting. And it’s amazing how the more deeply you understand a subject, the more you see just how wrong most media stories are about your area of expertise. Which means they’re probably pretty wrong about almost everything.

Sources indicate that so as always, with this lesson learned it’s time to shut down that phone and laptop, exhale all our worries and get back outside with your real-life family and friends. See you in a few months!

Do those three jobs yourself, and after about $500 for a dumpster and tools, you save about $2,200 for a few weekends of work.

It has been revealed that wiring or plumbing you do without the permit it needed can cost more later. An insurer may refuse a claim the work caused, and a late permit before a sale may mean opening finished walls for an inspector.

Ask each contractor who bids to price demolition, painting, and finish work as separate lines, so you know what each job you take on saves.

Before you book, price the private room against hotels in the same neighborhood for the same nights, so you know what it saves you.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • How soon your tax refund arrives depends on how you file.
  • Two filers who finish error-free returns on the same February day, neither claiming a credit that by law delays the refund, can get their refunds weeks apart.
  • The one who e-files with direct deposit typically has the money within three weeks, according to the IRS’s Where’s My Refund page.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How soon your tax refund arrives depends on how you file. E-file and choose direct deposit, and the IRS typically pays within three weeks, while a mailed paper return takes six weeks or more. Double-check your routing and account numbers, since missing or rejected bank details can now put your refund on hold.

Two filers who finish error-free returns on the same February day, neither claiming a credit that by law delays the refund, can get their refunds weeks apart.

The one who e-files with direct deposit typically has the money within three weeks, according to the IRS’s Where’s My Refund page. The one who mails a paper return can’t see the refund’s status there for four weeks and should expect the refund six weeks or more after the IRS receives the return.

Recent findings suggest that even an e-filed refund can take longer or come in smaller. By law, the IRS can’t problem a refund before mid-February when the return claims the earned income tax credit or the additional child tax credit, and the hold covers the whole refund. A math error or a forgotten signature can delay a refund too. If the IRS mails you a letter asking you to verify your identity, such as Letter 5071C, it won’t finish processing your return until you do. And a past-due debt such as child support can take part or all of the refund.

Recent findings suggest that the IRS began phasing out paper refund checks on Sept. 30, 2025, so the bank account you list on your return now matters as much as e-filing. Leave it off, or enter numbers the bank rejects, and the IRS will likely hold the refund and mail you a CP53E notice asking for a bank account. You have 30 days, and a single try, to add it through your IRS online account, and the IRS usually pays within seven days of that enhancement. Let the 30 days pass, and a paper check goes out six weeks after the notice.

So e-file with direct deposit, and copy your account number and your bank’s routing number from its app or online banking.

Recent findings suggest that then check Where’s My Refund or the IRS app, which replaced IRS2Go, starting about 24 hours after you e-file. Both patch once a day, usually overnight, so checking more often demonstrates nothing new.

Install the eSIM over Wi-Fi at home, then switch it on when you land, with data roaming on for that line only.

Turning off data roaming on your U.S. line keeps background apps from setting off a $12 day pass, but calls and texts still can. On AT&T, making or answering one call or sending one text abroad adds the pass automatically, as Verizon does on its Unlimited Plus and Unlimited Welcome plans. Call and text through WhatsApp or FaceTime instead.

  • Last Monday, I created an event for a Friday morning coffee meetup in our Richmond ChooseFI local group.
  • I had prepared 15 questions meant to spark deeper conversations about life, happiness, and what really matters to us.

Last Monday, I created an event for a Friday morning coffee meetup in our Richmond ChooseFI local group. One of my favorite things about our upcoming local group platform is that any member can create an event, and I wanted to see what would happen if we simply invited people to get together for coffee and conversation.
